1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight adds a second guard to d5, eyes e4 and prepares castling. Black commits to nothing, which also means White decides the character of the game, from a pin on the knight to a fianchettoed bishop or a quiet central set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn, so Black can take on c4 later and try to keep the extra pawn. The price is a tight position with the c8-bishop shut in behind e6 for a long time; the reward is a very solid centre and rich, double-edged play if White goes after the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Tarrasch Defence, Pseudo-Tarrasch
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once. After the exchange on d5 Black accepts an isolated d-pawn in return for free piece play. Because White's queen's knight is still at home, White can choose between the main-line set-up and an independent one, so Black gives White more say.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5.strategy: Resolves the tension in the centre and forces the question: Black must recapture and accept an isolated d-pawn, or lose time elsewhere. White now plays against that pawn with a clear structural target, while Black has to make its piece activity count.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the tension in the centre instead of resolving it at once. White can still capture on d5 later with the knight in play, but leaves Black to choose how the centre is released.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and frees the f1-bishop, a quiet and solid choice. It leaves the tension in the centre unresolved and lets Black release it on its own terms, so White gets a safe but unambitious game with no structural trump.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn, the idea of the whole line: Black takes an isolated d-pawn, but the c8-bishop is freed, the e-file opens and every piece gets a lively square. The pawn is a weakness to keep guarded and a springboard for central play.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops, but does not recapture on d5: 5.dxe6 Bxe6 6.dxc5 leaves White a clean pawn ahead, and Black's lead in development does not pay for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which is exposed on d5: a knight to c3 attacks it with tempo. Material stays level, but Black spends time retreating the queen while White develops.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.g.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop against the isolated d-pawn, the standard way of pressuring it. White keeps the kingside compact and the pieces flexible; Black gets free development and has to use it before the pressure on d5 builds.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.B.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Tarrasch Defence, Pseudo-Tarrasch Bishop Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.B.strategy: Develops with tempo: the exchange opened the diagonal to the queen, so Black must answer the bishop first. It works for quick development rather than against the isolated d-pawn, which this bishop does not pressure; the real test of the pawn comes with other pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.N.strategy: Develops the queen's knight with an attack on d5, the pawn the exchange isolated, so the pressure starts at once. White keeps both the fianchetto and a quiet build-up in hand and plays against the pawn without hurry.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.cxd5 exd5 5.g.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre, adding pressure on d4 and e5. Black's game rests on quick, harmonious development, which is what the isolated d-pawn pays for.

Covers d5 before the white bishop reaches the long diagonal and develops towards castling. The queen's knight stays at home, free to choose its square, so Black decides the shape of the centre a little later.

Prepares castling, but does nothing for d5: once the bishop reaches g2 and the f3-knight steps aside, the pawn is attacked, and Black will need a knight to guard it. Sound, but it leaves the isolated pawn for later.

Completes the fianchetto. The bishop stands behind the f3-knight for now but aims at d5, and the pressure grows as soon as that knight steps aside; the king is also one move from castling. White plays patiently against the isolated pawn.
Develops the queen's knight with a direct attack on d5, so the pressure on the isolated pawn starts before the bishop is out. White keeps the structure as it is and goes on building slowly.
Takes the pawn, but Black wins it back at once with the bishop and may first push the d-pawn to d4 for space. White gives up the central tension that its pressure on d5 depends on.

Guards d5 a second time and develops, so the pawn is covered when the g2-bishop's diagonal opens. Black heads for castling with a compact position; the isolated pawn must never be left short of protection.

Prepares castling and brings the bishop out of the way, keeping the same set-up in a different order. For now d5 has only the queen to guard it, so the knight must come to f6 soon, before the bishop's diagonal opens.

Trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the c-file, but the knight recaptures on d4 and the bishop on g2 then bears down on d5. Black must guard the pawn at once, and only then is the exchange sound.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the second knight to its natural square, adds control of d5 and e4 and prepares the e4 break. White commits to nothing else yet: a pin, an exchange on d5 or quiet development all remain open, and Black has to be ready for each of them.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Traditional Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6-knight to the queen, tying down one of the defenders of d5 and making Black's freeing plans harder. Black will want to break the pin and get the king safe; White hopes to keep a space edge and a long manoeuvring game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop towards d5 and the queenside, trading a quick centre for lasting long-diagonal pressure. White's c4 pawn can be left loose, because opening the diagonal is worth more; Black gets a solid centre but must live with the bishop for the whole game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: Quiet and solid: it guards d4 and opens the f1-bishop, but it shuts the c1-bishop in behind its own pawns, the same problem Black has on the other wing. White gives up both the pin and the long-diagonal pressure, so the game becomes slow and Black equalises easily.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 h6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the g5-bishop at once: retreat and keep the pin, or exchange for the knight. With White's queen's knight still at home, the immediate exchange on f6 puts no pressure on d5, so Black can ask the question safely.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4+.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Vienna Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4+.strategy: Counters the pin with a pin of its own: the check forces a block, and a knight arriving on c3 stands pinned to the king, so White cannot simply carry on with its centre plans. The game becomes sharper and more double-edged.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with the c-pawn, so the f6-knight is no longer essential to its defence and the pin loses much of its sting. Black accepts a cramped position with the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, in return for a very solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the centre without getting a concession first. Black cannot expect to keep the pawn: White regains it in its own time with a developing move and builds a strong centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7.strategy: Puts the bishop behind the pinned knight, so the pin loses its sting and castling is one move away. If White takes on f6, Black recaptures with the bishop. A solid way to meet the bishop on g5: the centre stays firm and Black develops without concessions.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to guard c4, so ...dxc4 would win no pawn, and keeps the e-pawn free for a solid centre. White keeps the bishop on g5 bearing down on f6; the price is that the knight on d2 can be pinned against the king by ...Qa5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and adds pressure on d5 without guarding c4. If Black takes the pawn and holds it with ...b5, White strikes with a central advance against the pinned knight. The sharper choice here: a pawn offered for the initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, the quiet way to keep the centre and castle soon. It leaves c4 unguarded: Black can take it and chase the recapturing bishop with ...b5, gaining queenside space at the cost of loosening that wing.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.strategy: Adds a second defender to f6, so the pin by the bishop on g5 costs Black nothing, and supports a later central break with ...e5. Black settles for a compact c6-d5-e6 pawn chain, at the price of a light-squared bishop that stays shut in behind e6.

Breaks the pin by placing the bishop behind the knight and prepares castling. Black postpones the fight for the centre and accepts a slightly passive position in return for a sound structure and easy development.

Puts the question to the bishop at once: retreating keeps the pin, but taking on f6 lets Black recapture with the queen and enjoy the two bishops. The pawn move develops nothing, and the light-squared bishop is still shut in behind e6.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.strategy: Backs up d4 with a second guard, frees the king's bishop and prepares castling, while the knight on d2 holds c4. A patient, solid set-up: White keeps the bishop on g5 pinning down f6 and aims for a slow build-up in the centre rather than quick tactics.

Resolves the tension at once and removes the option of taking on c4. Black has to recapture with a pawn, because the f6 knight is pinned against the queen, and the centre turns stable and strategic with little room for early tactics.

Trades the bishop for the knight and with it the pin it has built up, handing Black the bishop pair. The other knight recaptures on f6 with a good square, so White has little to show for the exchange.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.strategy: Wins the c4 pawn back with check: Black cannot hold it by force, so White spends no tempo regaining it and keeps the bishop on g5 bearing on the f6 knight. Black has to find the least awkward way to block the check, and White's queen reaches an active square.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and prepares to take the centre instead of rushing to regain the pawn. The knight also covers b5, so ...b5 would only drop a pawn to Nxb5 instead of holding c4. White gets space and quick development, and the c4 pawn is regained later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.e.strategy: Opens the king's bishop to take the pawn back on c4, a quiet and sound way to regain it. Black can hold the pawn for a while with ...b5, so White does not recover it at once and has to wait for the queenside to open.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.strategy: Blocks the check with a pawn, so no piece is misplaced, and prepares ...b5 to chase the queen once it recaptures on c4. Black accepts that the extra pawn is gone and aims for a solid queenside and quick development.
Blocks the check with the queen's knight, which develops it but leaves it pinned on d7 until the queen moves. White regains c4 without fuss, and after a trade on f6 that knight cannot recapture.

Blocks the check with the light-squared bishop, which is pinned there against the king for the moment. The pawn on c4 falls anyway, and the bishop's next step to c6 is the only point, so Black has gained little for the time spent.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Traditional Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.strategy: Recaptures and puts the queen on an active diagonal, eyeing the e6 pawn, with White ahead in development. The queen is exposed to a pawn push on the queenside, so it will need a good square soon, but the Queen's Gambit pawn is regained at once.
Develops the king's bishop but does not win back c4: 6...b5 attacks the queen, which must move again, and Black keeps the extra pawn with no real compensation for White.
Develops the knight but leaves c4 alone: 6...b5 attacks the queen and keeps the pawn, and the knight cannot take on b5 without losing a piece for two pawns. White loses time and the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7.strategy: The classical set-up: the bishop clears the way for castling and keeps the pawn chain intact. Black stays solid and waits, the c8-bishop remaining the long-term task; White has the freer development and a small space edge to play with.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, before White has castled, aiming for free piece play. The cost is a structure in which Black often ends up with an isolated or hanging central pawn pair that White can target, so the dynamic activity has to make up for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c6.strategy: Backs d5 with the c-pawn and builds a very solid chain, giving up the ...c5 break. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 for now; Black keeps the option of taking on c4 and holding the pawn, which leads to sharp, double-edged play.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to free the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal without a pawn break. It is slower than the main set-ups: d5 gets less support, and after the exchange on d5 a check on b5 has to be answered with care.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and attacks d5 a second time, so Black will want the fianchettoed bishop as a further defender of the pawn there. White keeps the choice between exchanging in the centre and a quiet build-up with the king's bishop and castling.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3.strategy: Meets the fianchetto with a fianchetto of its own: the bishop on b2 will back the d4 pawn and look at the centre. The set-up is solid and flexible but quiet, with less pressure on d5 than the knight move brings; neither side has a clear edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the king's bishop at once, but it adds no pressure to d5. Black can resolve the tension by capturing on c4, after which the bishop recaptures on an active diagonal and the game is calm and roughly level.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3 B.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: both queen's bishops head for the long diagonal behind their d-pawns, so the game becomes a fight over the first pawn break in the centre.

Prepares castling and keeps Black's plans open. The queen's bishop still has to find its square and the fight for the centre is not yet decided, but nothing is weakened and the pieces stay harmonious.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3 c.strategy: Attacks d4 at once, trying to take the initiative in the centre before White's bishop reaches the long diagonal. The price is a looser centre, with the queen's bishop still undeveloped and the d5 pawn to watch.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3 B.strategy: Develops the king's bishop on the diagonal aimed at h7 and backs a later e4 advance. It prepares castling and keeps all of White's central plans open, while the pawns on b3 and e3 make a solid base.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop backs d4 and aims along the long diagonal, a solid and flexible set-up. It leaves the king's bishop to choose its square later, and the game becomes a fight over who breaks first in the centre.
Clears the tension in the centre at once. Black may recapture either way, and with Black's bishop already on the long diagonal, White gets a safe but rather drawish game with few chances to press.
Completes queenside development and supports the f6 knight and the e5 square. It prepares a pawn break in the centre, at the price of a slightly cramped queenside.
Prepares castling and supports the f6 knight, completing the kingside development with no weakness. The queen's knight stays flexible, and Black is ready to meet whichever central plan White chooses.

Challenges d4 at once, opening lines for the pieces while the bishop on b7 looks along the long diagonal. The centre becomes less stable and d5 may need protection, but Black takes the initiative in the middle instead of waiting.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop to the long diagonal, where it defends d5 and stands ready for when the centre opens. For now it looks at its own pawn, so it comes alive only after a central pawn break; in return Black gets a solid, flexible set-up that holds the centre without committing the king's bishop.

Places the bishop on the b8-h2 diagonal aiming at the kingside, but it is exposed on d6. Once the centre is opened, White can gain time by attacking it with a knight, so Black loses time while White develops.

Develops the king's bishop on its natural square and prepares castling. It does not fight for the centre yet, but it keeps the pawn structure solid and leaves the long diagonal free for the other bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the bishop to its best diagonal, where it eyes h7, and prepares castling, keeping the capture on d5 in reserve. White stays flexible and can choose its central plan after Black has shown the set-up, while the d6 bishop gets in the way of Black's own pieces.

Settles the tension in the centre. After the recapture with the e-pawn the symmetrical structure leaves the bishop on d6 exposed to a knight jump to b5, which wins White a tempo, while White's pieces are ready to develop freely.

Develops the king's bishop and prepares castling, but passively: from e2 it presses neither on the kingside nor on the centre. Black's d6 bishop keeps its active diagonal, and Black can finish development and challenge the centre in comfort.
Castles at once. The knight on f6 guards h7 against the bishop on d3, so the king is safe. Black keeps the central tension and chooses between a pawn break in the centre and capturing on c4 later.
Puts the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it defends d5 and waits for the centre to open. The f6 knight guards h7 against the bishop on d3, so Black can take its time over castling.

Brings the queen's knight into play, supporting f6 and the e5 square. A sound but slow way to develop: the queen's bishop is still undeveloped, and the d6 bishop remains exposed to a white knight jump to b5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Exchange Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre. The e6 pawn, which blocked the light-squared bishop, leaves, and the bishop gets its diagonal; the price is that the bishop on d6 can be attacked by a knight jump to b5, so Black has to be ready to lose a tempo.

Recaptures with the knight, which keeps the pawn on e6 and leaves White no pawn on d5 to attack. The knight in the centre can be hit by e4, so Black has to be ready to trade it or move it, and White gains space with tempo.

Ignores the pawn on d5: White plays dxe6 and Black can only retake with the f-pawn, ending a pawn down with a damaged kingside structure. Finishing the fianchetto cannot wait while the centre is open.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.Nc3.strategy: Brings out the knight and adds pressure on d5 and e4, reaching the classical set-up of this opening. White keeps every plan open, and the real contest is whether Black can free the light-squared bishop that the e6 pawn locks in.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it supports the d4 pawn and eyes the centre. The b3 pawn also firms up c4, so taking on c4 would only help White build a broad centre. A restrained plan, with less immediate pressure on d5 than the knight move.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop on the diagonal towards h7 and clears the way to castle, but commits it early. If Black takes on c4, the bishop recaptures after spending two moves to get there, so Black has gained a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Castles and completes the kingside. Black has no reason to hurry against a slow set-up: the usual plan is the pawn break against White's centre, which Black prepares by finishing development first and keeping the d5 pawn firm.

Challenges d4 at once, aiming to trade off White's centre and free the position before White's set-up is complete. The king is still in the centre while the tension resolves, and the pawn structure loosens as pawns come off.

Fianchettoes the queen's bishop so that it meets White's bishop on the long diagonal, which also frees the light-squared bishop the pawn on e6 would otherwise shut in. A solid, symmetrical plan, with the central pawn break kept in reserve.

Puts the bishop on its long diagonal at once and keeps the king's bishop flexible. It supports the d4 pawn and eyes the centre; White keeps the choice of where the other bishop goes, and the game becomes a quiet fight for space in the centre.

Develops the king's bishop on the diagonal aimed at h7 and prepares to castle. The bishop is now committed, which gives Black the chance to release the tension in the centre or to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and free it.

Adds a knight to the pressure on d5 and e4 while the queen's bishop still heads for the long diagonal. If Black takes on c4, White can retake with either the bishop or the b-pawn and pick the better structure, so the centre stays flexible.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Solves the problem of the light-squared bishop by fianchettoing it, where it can look along the long diagonal once the centre opens. Black commits to fighting for the centre with a pawn break or with captures on c4, not to a slow pawn chain on c6.

The thematic break: with the king safe, Black challenges the d4 pawn to open lines for active pieces. The tension in the centre then decides the game, and Black keeps the option of taking on c4 at a moment of its own choosing.

Takes the pawn now that White's bishop has committed to d3. If the bishop recaptures, it has needed two moves to reach c4 and Black has gained time; if the b-pawn recaptures, White gets a broad centre that Black can aim to undermine.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn before Black can build a full centre, forcing Black to decide the pawn structure. The tension between the c5 and d4 pawns then decides the game, and either side can end up with an isolated pawn and active pieces as compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5 5.Nc3.strategy: Brings the knight to the centre instead of resolving the tension, leaving Black to decide what happens on d4 and d5. White keeps a flexible pawn structure and the option of exchanging on d5 later, at the price of giving Black a free choice of set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5 5.dxc5.strategy: Releases the tension by taking the pawn, but Black retakes with the bishop, which develops to an active square in one move. White has given up the pawn on d4 that held Black's centre, and Black's pieces gain freedom.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping the knight on f6 and opening the diagonal of the light-squared bishop. Black gets a duo of pawns on c5 and d5 against the d4 pawn. If White later takes on c5, Black has an isolated d-pawn but active piece play.

Recaptures with the knight, keeping the pawn on e6 so that no isolated or hanging pawns arise. The knight is a target for e4 and for the bishop on c4, so Black has to use it actively and not lose time.

Recaptures with the queen, which comes out early and is hit at once by a knight on c3, so Black loses a tempo. The pawn structure stays healthy, but White gains time for development in a position where Black is not yet ready.

Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and gives the knight possible jumps to b5 and d5. White's pieces aim at Black's central pawns, which must be defended, and the game turns on whether Black's active pieces compensate for the structure.

Gives up the central tension and aims at the structure: once Black regains the pawn, d5 stands alone without pawn neighbours, a lasting target. Black gets open lines and active pieces for it, so the game is a contest of weakness against activity.

Checks at once, forcing Black to block. It develops with tempo, but the bishop has little to aim at beyond trading off Black's light-squared bishop, and the symmetrical structure gives White little. A solid, level choice.
Takes the b5 square away from White's bishop and knight, but spends a tempo on a flank move while White's pieces take over the centre and the pawns on c5 and d5 are left to be challenged.

Develops the knight with pressure on d4 and keeps the pawns on c5 and d5 where they are. The structure is symmetrical and either side can end up with an isolated pawn, so the game is decided by piece activity.

Develops the bishop and prepares castling without committing the queen's knight. It lets White decide the tension first: if White takes on c5 the bishop retakes, leaving Black an isolated d-pawn but active pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling and leaves the choice open: Black can take on c4 later or keep the centre closed. It is the flexible way to develop while White decides how to handle the bishop and the c4 pawn, and the dark-squared bishop stays out of harm.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6.strategy: Shields d5 with a pawn against the long diagonal, so the g2-bishop meets a wall. Black accepts a compact but cramped position with the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, in return for a solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+.strategy: Checks to force a concession in White's set-up: the c1-bishop, usually, has to take an awkward square on d2. The cost is that the bishop may have to be traded or retreat later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: Meets the check by developing the queen's bishop and offering the trade, keeping the fianchetto plan. The bishop is not best placed on d2, but Black's bishop must now decide whether to retreat or to exchange, so the check costs Black time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Nc.strategy: Blocks the check with a knight that is then pinned against the king. Black can add to the pressure on it, and if the bishop takes on c3 White may be left with doubled pawns, so White has to unpin soon.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Nb.strategy: Blocks the check with the other knight, but it is pinned against the king and shuts in the bishop on c1. Black takes on c4 at once, as the pinned knight cannot recapture, and White is left a pawn down with only some pressure on the long diagonal.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: Retreats instead of exchanging, keeping the bishop pair at the cost of a tempo. White's bishop is not on the best square on d2, so the tempo is not a high price. A solid choice that keeps the position closed and Black's structure healthy.

Trades bishops at once, giving up the bishop pair for a simple, level position. White recaptures with a knight or the queen, pieces that would rather stand elsewhere, so Black has no problems but no advantage either.

Defends the bishop on b4 with a pawn, so Black can keep it there instead of retreating or trading. White's bishop on d2 stays awkwardly placed, and the price is a pawn on a5 that is a slight weakness on the queenside.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop sits behind the f3 knight, looking at the long diagonal, and the king gets a safe home after castling. White plans long-term queenside and centre pressure while Black holds a solid structure.

Puts the queen on c2, where it supports the c4 pawn and prepares e4. White keeps the fianchetto available, and if Black takes on c4 the queen can recapture at once, so White loses no time in the fight for the centre.
Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and e4, but it blocks the c-pawn and takes the c3 square from the bishop on d2. Sound but a little clumsy, as White's pieces get in each other's way.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop on the long diagonal presses on d5 and the queenside, a pressure that grows once the f3-knight moves. White trades a quick central grab for lasting pressure, with the king a move from castling.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and e4, but it blocks the c-pawn, and the g3 move has not yet been justified by the bishop. Sound, but Black gets time to castle and to choose when to release the tension.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7 5.Qc2.strategy: Puts the queen on c2 to support the c4 pawn and prepare e4. The queen becomes a target if Black takes on c4, because after Qxc4 Black can gain time with ...b5, so the move is sound but slightly loosening.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop, the move behind the whole set-up. Black's c6 and d5 pawns shield the long diagonal for now, so White's pressure is slow and positional: build behind the pawns, keep the king safe, and wait for the centre to open.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Nbd2.strategy: Backs up c4 and e4 with the knight so that ...dxc4 can be recaptured by a piece. The knight takes the d2 square from the queen's bishop, which then has to wait for b3 before it can come out.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and e4, but it stands in front of the c-pawn. Sound but unambitious: Black can take on c4 or build quietly, and White has not yet put the bishop on its diagonal.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Takes the pawn and tries to keep it with ...b5, which the c6 pawn supports. The capture also opens the long diagonal in front of White's bishop. If White regains the pawn, Black has at least gained time; if not, Black must hold the weakened queenside.

The solid developing move: the knight supports the centre and prepares a bishop to d6 or a break in the centre. Black keeps the compact pawn triangle on c6, d5 and e6 and the choice between taking on c4 and keeping the tension.

Develops the bishop and prepares castling, keeping the compact pawn triangle on c6, d5 and e6. A safe, slightly passive set-up in which Black waits for White to commit and can still take on c4 at a good moment.
